summary:
Central Sulawesi stands under the national framework of Indonesia. The sources record no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement specific to this province, so a visitor is assessed against the national position with no documented sub-national deviation.

Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in that province. Nothing in the sources indicates equivalent provincial religious penalties operating in Central Sulawesi.

Indonesian law provides no explicit legal protection of transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a conservative petition seeking to criminalise homosexuality and extramarital sex by five votes to four, declining to add those offences to the Penal Code. Legal gender change requires sex reassignment surgery together with judicial approval, which determines the documents a trans visitor can present to Indonesian authorities on arrival.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a wave running from 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than fifteen women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage of the assaults shared online. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to the wave of vigilante attacks. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Venue raids are a further enforcement form. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a gay party and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
A researcher cited by The Diplomat documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes in Indonesia since 2016, which sets the social climate a trans visitor enters in Central Sulawesi alongside the legal position.

A global survey reported in the sources finds that discrimination and harassment against transgender people are not uncommon in Indonesia while direct violence is rare. That general finding sits against the specific, dated evidence of the July 2026 mob assaults and the June 2025 villa raid, so the lower baseline should not be read as an absence of acute incidents.

Provincial variation is the main comparative axis within Indonesia. Aceh and South Sumatra carry their own criminalisation of same-sex conduct, and Aceh's caning of February 2025 was imposed under provincial religious law, whereas Central Sulawesi has no recorded equivalent. The national penal code and the morality provisions remain the operative layer everywhere else.

Amnesty International characterised the June 2025 villa operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, noting that the gathering broke no law. The organisation's assessment is the clearest official-adjacent commentary on how far enforcement currently exceeds the text of the statute.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment and can be pushed into sex work. This is a resident-facing economic consequence of the absence of anti-discrimination protection rather than a direct legal penalty.

Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitutional Court's 5-4 rejection on 14 December 2017 of a petition to criminalise homosexuality and extramarital sex left the Penal Code unchanged on those points, although the 2022 code later introduced the extra-marital sex offence that took effect on 2 January 2026.

Legal gender change for residents requires sex reassignment surgery and judicial approval. The procedure is therefore gated by both medical and court processes, and the resulting marker is what appears in identity documents used domestically and at the border.

Provincial moral laws operate as an enforcement layer in parts of Indonesia, and Aceh's caning sentence of February 2025 was issued under provincial religious law. Whether Central Sulawesi maintains its own moral regulations is not stated in the sources.

Enforcement of the national morality provisions inside Central Sulawesi is not sourced. The examples available (the Puncak villa raid, the Bogor assaults) are drawn from other provinces and cities and illustrate national patterns rather than local practice.

The full scope of the 14 to 16 July 2026 attacks is unresolved: the sources itemise more than fifteen victims in one city and describe a nationwide wave without a total count or a list of affected provinces.

The circumstances of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla's death in custody remain disputed and unresolved. His mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police deny that violence was used, and no independent finding is recorded in the inventory.
